chapter_title: Simulating Robots with Gazebo and URDF
chapter_summary:
Before you deploy code on a real robot, you should test it in simulation. **Gazebo** is the 3D physics simulator that integrates with ROS. It simulates rigid body dynamics, collisions, sensors (cameras, LiDAR, IMU), and actuators (motors, servos). Gazebo allows you to develop and debug your robot's behavior in a safe, repeatable environment before risking physical hardware.

To simulate a robot in Gazebo, you need a **URDF** (Unified Robot Description Format) file. URDF is an XML format that describes the robot's physical structure: its links (rigid bodies), joints (connections between links), and their geometric and inertial properties.

A simple URDF for a mobile robot:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<robot name="my_robot">
  <!-- Base link -->
  <link name="base_link">
    <visual>
      <geometry>
        <box size="0.5 0.3 0.1" />
      </geometry>
      <material name="blue">
        <color rgba="0 0 1 1" />
      </material>
    </visual>
    <collision>
      <geometry>
        <box size="0.5 0.3 0.1" />
      </geometry>
    </collision>
    <inertial>
      <mass value="1.0" />
      <inertia ixx="0.01" ixy="0" ixz="0" iyy="0.01" iyz="0" izz="0.01" />
    </inertial>
  </link>
  
  <!-- Right wheel -->
  <link name="right_wheel">
    <visual>
      <geometry>
        <cylinder radius="0.05" length="0.05" />
      </geometry>
      <material name="black">
        <color rgba="0 0 0 1" />
      </material>
    </visual>
    <collision>
      <geometry>
        <cylinder radius="0.05" length="0.05" />
      </geometry>
    </collision>
    <inertial>
      <mass value="0.1" />
      <inertia ixx="0.0001" ixy="0" ixz="0" iyy="0.0001" iyz="0" izz="0.0001" />
    </inertial>
  </link>
  
  <joint name="right_wheel_joint" type="continuous">
    <parent link="base_link" />
    <child link="right_wheel" />
    <origin xyz="0.2 -0.15 0" rpy="0 1.5708 0" />
    <axis xyz="0 0 1" />
  </joint>
  
  <!-- Left wheel (similar structure) -->
  <link name="left_wheel">
    <!-- ... same as right wheel ... -->
  </link>
  
  <joint name="left_wheel_joint" type="continuous">
    <parent link="base_link" />
    <child link="left_wheel" />
    <origin xyz="0.2 0.15 0" rpy="0 1.5708 0" />
    <axis xyz="0 0 1" />
  </joint>
  
  <!-- Gazebo plugin for differential drive -->
  <gazebo>
    <plugin name="differential_drive_controller" filename="libgazebo_ros_diff_drive.so">
      <legacyMode>false</legacyMode>
      <alwaysOn>true</alwaysOn>
      <updateRate>50</updateRate>
      <leftJoint>left_wheel_joint</leftJoint>
      <rightJoint>right_wheel_joint</rightJoint>
      <wheelSeparation>0.3</wheelSeparation>
      <wheelDiameter>0.1</wheelDiameter>
      <torque>0.5</torque>
      <commandTopic>cmd_vel</commandTopic>
      <odometryTopic>odom</odometryTopic>
      <odometryFrame>odom</odometryFrame>
      <robotBaseFrame>base_link</robotBaseFrame>
    </plugin>
  </gazebo>
</robot>
```

Key URDF elements:
- `<link>`: A rigid body with visual, collision, and inertial properties.
- `<joint>`: A connection between two links. Types include `fixed`, `revolute`, `continuous`, `prismatic`, and `floating`.
- `<visual>`: The geometry used for visualization (in RViz and Gazebo).
- `<collision>`: The geometry used for collision detection (often a simplified version of the visual geometry).
- `<inertial>`: The mass and inertia tensor of the link. Required for accurate physics simulation.
- `<gazebo>`: Gazebo-specific properties, including plugins that connect Gazebo to ROS.

**Gazebo plugins:**
Gazebo plugins are shared libraries that add functionality to the simulation. The `gazebo_ros_diff_drive` plugin, for example, subscribes to `/cmd_vel` and applies forces to the wheels to make the robot move. It also publishes odometry data on `/odom`. This means that once the plugin is configured, you can control the simulated robot with the same ROS topics you would use for a real robot.

**Loading the URDF in Gazebo:**

```xml
<!-- launch/robot_gazebo.launch -->
<launch>
  <!-- Load the URDF into the parameter server -->
  <param name="robot_description" textfile="$(find my_first_robot)/urdf/my_robot.urdf" />
  
  <!-- Start Gazebo with an empty world -->
  <include file="$(find gazebo_ros)/launch/empty_world.launch" />
  
  <!-- Spawn the robot in Gazebo -->
  <node pkg="gazebo_ros" type="spawn_model" name="spawn_robot" 
        args="-param robot_description -urdf -model my_robot -x 0 -y 0 -z 0.1" />
  
  <!-- Start robot state publisher -->
  <node pkg="robot_state_publisher" type="robot_state_publisher" name="robot_state_publisher" />
</launch>
```

Launch the simulation:
```bash
roslaunch my_first_robot robot_gazebo.launch
```

Then control the robot:
```bash
rostopic pub /cmd_vel geometry_msgs/Twist "linear:
  x: 0.5
  y: 0.0
  z: 0.0
angular:
  x: 0.0
  y: 0.0
  z: 0.2"
```

The robot should move forward and turn in the Gazebo simulation.

**Safety note:** Gazebo is a physics simulator, not a video game. It uses realistic physics models, which means robots can tip over, collide, and behave unexpectedly. Always start with simple robots and low velocities. When you transition from simulation to a real robot, expect differences: real motors have friction, real sensors have noise, and real environments have unpredictable elements.

screens.title: Simulating Robots with Gazebo and URDF
screens.subtitle: Describe robots with URDF, spawn them in Gazebo, and bridge sensors and actuators to ROS

narration.text: Simulation is the safest place to test robot designs and control code before touching hardware. In this lesson you will learn what URDF is — an XML description that specifies links, joints, visual and collision geometry, and inertial properties — and how Gazebo uses that description to run a physics-accurate virtual robot. You will also see how gazebo_ros plugins translate ROS topics like /cmd_vel into forces on wheel joints, and how odometry and sensor topics flow back into the ROS ecosystem. A concrete example we will use is a differential-drive mobile base: two cylindrical wheels, a rectangular base, and a plugin that subscribes to velocity commands and publishes odometry. Practically, simulation lets you iterate quickly, test safety limits, and reproduce edge cases without risking hardware. A common misconception is that simulation always matches reality; in practice you must expect differences in friction, sensor noise, and timing. As you explore the chapter, imagine how the URDF maps to the robot’s physical parts and how plugin settings affect responsiveness. By the end you will be able to write a simple URDF, spawn it in Gazebo, and control it using standard ROS topics.

keyIdea.title: Why simulate first
keyIdea.text: Gazebo + URDF give a repeatable, safe environment to validate robot design, control, and sensors before deploying on hardware.

screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do and why it matters

narration.text: These learning objectives lay out the practical skills you will build. First, you will understand the URDF format: what links and joints represent and why visual, collision, and inertial tags are separate. This understanding matters because URDF tells both the simulator and your TF tree how the robot is structured. Second, you will write a simple URDF for a mobile robot with wheels and a sensor. Writing such a file teaches you how geometric primitives and inertial properties change a robot’s simulated behavior. Third, you will launch a robot in Gazebo and control it via ROS topics. Running the launch file shows how the simulation lifecycle is managed and how control messages map to motion. Finally, you will use gazebo_ros plugins to connect Gazebo sensors and actuators to ROS topics. Plugins are the bridge between simulation internals and ROS, and learning to configure them means your code will work with both simulated and physical robots. Each objective includes a small demonstration step you can do in the lab to verify competency.

screens.title: What is URDF and what does it describe?
screens.subtitle: URDF is the XML blueprint of a robot's structure used by ROS and Gazebo

narration.text: URDF stands for Unified Robot Description Format and it is the canonical XML-based way to describe a robot’s kinematic and physical properties for ROS and simulators like Gazebo. At its core URDF represents links, which are rigid bodies, and joints, which connect those bodies and constrain their relative motion. Each link typically includes three sections: visual geometry for rendering, collision geometry for physics, and inertial data for mass and inertia tensor. Visual geometry can be detailed because it only affects appearance. Collision geometry should be simplified so the physics engine can compute contacts efficiently. Inertial information — mass and the inertia tensor — is essential for realistic dynamics: if you omit or approximate it poorly, the robot may behave unnaturally in simulation. A concrete example is a mobile base: the base_link has a box visual and collision entry, and each wheel is modeled as a cylinder with a continuous joint. A common misconception is that URDF is only for visualization. In reality, URDF directly influences controllers, simulation stability, and TF transforms. When you author a URDF, think in physical terms: how heavy is each part, where is its center of mass, and which geometry matters for collisions versus appearance. That mindset leads to better, safer simulations.

keyIdea.title: URDF purpose
keyIdea.text: URDF is both a visual blueprint and a physics-aware description: links, joints, visuals, collisions, and inertial values drive simulation and TF.

content.html:
Core Concept
URDF structure

URDF models the robot as a tree of links and joints. Visual tags affect rendering; collision tags affect physics; inertial tags affect dynamics. Keep collision geometry simple.

Links
Rigid bodies with visual, collision, and inertial entries.
Joints
Define motion constraints between links; types include fixed, revolute, continuous, prismatic, and floating.
Visual vs Collision
Use detailed meshes for visuals and simple primitives for collision to save compute.
Concrete URDF snippet
<link name="base_link">   <visual>     <geometry>      <box size="0.5 0.3 0.1" />     </geometry>   </visual> </link>
Example
Model a rectangular base and two cylindrical wheels. Specify inertial mass for each link so physics responds correctly when accelerating or colliding.
Key takeaway
URDF ties visual, collision, and inertial data to physical behavior; treat each intentionally.

screens.title: A minimal mobile robot URDF
screens.subtitle: An annotated URDF snippet for a differential-drive base

narration.text: Let's walk through a minimal URDF for a differential-drive robot and explain each section so you can write your own. The file starts with a robot tag and contains link elements such as base_link and wheel links. Each link includes visual and collision geometry: for a mobile base you might use a box for both visual and collision, while wheels are cylinders. Inertial entries include mass and an inertia tensor; these let the physics engine compute accelerations and torque responses. Joints connect links: for wheels use continuous joints so rotation is unbounded, and specify parent and child link names plus the joint axis. The URDF in the chapter also shows a gazebo plugin section. That gazebo block is allowed inside the robot element and configures a differential-drive plugin with left and right joint names, wheel separation, wheel diameter, and topics like cmd_vel and odom. A concrete example from the chapter uses left_wheel_joint and right_wheel_joint and sets wheelSeparation to 0.3 and wheelDiameter to 0.1. A frequent mistake is forgetting to match joint names between your URDF and plugin configuration — double-check names. Try creating the minimal URDF, spawn it, and iterate on inertial values until the base behaves realistically.

keyIdea.title: Author with intent
keyIdea.text: Write URDF with correct joint names and sensible inertial values; plugin configurations must reference those exact names.

content.html:
Code walkthrough
Minimal mobile URDF
<robot name="my_robot">
  <link name="base_link">
    <visual>
      <geometry><box size="0.5 0.3 0.1" /></geometry>
    </visual>
  </link>

  <link name="right_wheel">...</link>

  <joint name="right_wheel_joint" type="continuous">
    <parent link="base_link" />
    <child link="right_wheel" />
    <axis xyz="0 0 1" />
  </joint>

  <gazebo>...plugin configuration...</gazebo>
</robot>
Annotated notes
  • base_link: The robot’s frame of reference. Provide visual, collision, and inertial entries.
  • wheel links: Cylinders with small mass; include collision and visual separately.
  • joint type continuous: Use for wheels to allow unlimited rotation. Match joint names in plugin configs.
  • gazebo plugin: Configure leftJoint, rightJoint, wheelSeparation, wheelDiameter, cmd_vel and odom topics so controllers work.
Example values
wheelSeparation 0.3, wheelDiameter 0.1, torque 0.5, updateRate 50
Common mistake
Mismatched joint names between URDF and plugin prevents motion. Verify names exactly.

screens.title: Visual vs Collision vs Inertial geometry
screens.subtitle: Why each geometry type exists and how to choose them

narration.text: Understanding the difference between visual, collision, and inertial geometry prevents performance problems and unrealistic behavior. Visual geometry is what you see in RViz or Gazebo; it can be detailed for aesthetics because it does not impact physics performance directly. Collision geometry is used by the physics engine to detect contacts and compute forces. For collision you should choose simple primitives such as boxes, cylinders, or spheres; simplified collision shapes reduce C P U usage and avoid noisy contact calculations. Inertial geometry is not geometry per se but the inertial properties — mass and components of the inertia tensor — that let the physics engine compute accelerations and torques. If you set inertial values incorrectly, a robot may tip, spin, or respond sluggishly. A practical example: give the base_link a modest mass and accurate inertia approximations so controllers produce expected accelerations, but model an arm’s collision boxes simply to keep simulation fast. A common misconception is to reuse the detailed visual mesh for collision. That leads to slow simulation and unstable contacts. Instead, keep visuals rich and collisions simple, and always include inertial entries. When in doubt, test with reduced complexity and increase detail only when necessary.

keyIdea.title: Right geometry for the right job
keyIdea.text: Use detailed visuals for appearance, simplified collision shapes for physics, and accurate inertial values for realistic dynamics.

content.html:
Comparison
Visual vs Collision vs Inertial
Visual: detailed meshes for realistic rendering. No heavy physics cost but large files increase load time.
Collision: primitives or simplified meshes used by the physics engine. Keep simple to speed up simulation.
Inertial: mass and inertia tensor values that determine how the body accelerates and rotates under force.
Concrete scenario

You have a heavy rectangular base and two small wheels. For visuals, a detailed mesh makes the robot look correct. For collision, model the base as a single box and each wheel as a cylinder. For inertial entries, set the base mass to a realistic number and smaller masses for the wheels; include inertia values that approximate the distribution of mass. This balance gives stable contacts and realistic acceleration.

Pro tip
When in doubt, test with simplified collision shapes and tune inertia until the behavior matches expectations.
Common mistake
Using complex visual meshes for collision causes slow simulation and unstable contact physics.

screens.title: How Gazebo plugins connect to ROS topics
screens.subtitle: Plugins translate ROS messages into simulation forces and publish sensor outputs

narration.text: Gazebo plugins are shared libraries that extend the simulator with robot-specific behavior and a bridge to ROS topics. The gazebo_ros_diff_drive plugin is a common example: it subscribes to velocity commands such as /cmd_vel, converts those commands into forces or torques applied to wheel joints, and publishes odometry on /odom. This means you can use the same command messages in simulation that you would on a real robot. Plugins can also publish sensor topics such as /scan for LiDAR or /camera/image_raw for cameras by forwarding Gazebo’s simulated sensor outputs into ROS message streams. A practical configuration includes parameters like leftJoint and rightJoint names, wheelSeparation, wheelDiameter, torque limits, and an updateRate which controls how often the plugin applies forces. A common misconception is that plugins magically make simulation identical to reality; they approximate. Plugin parameters and physics settings still need tuning for performance and realism. When configuring plugins, make sure joint names exactly match those in your URDF and start with conservative torque and velocity limits. This incremental approach reduces unexpected behaviors in the simulated robot. How Gazebo plugins connect to ROS topics means gazebo plugins map ros topics to simulation behavior and publish simulated sensor data back to ros topics.. In practical terms, plugins translate ros messages into simulation forces and publish sensor outputs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Plugin role
keyIdea.text: Gazebo plugins map ROS topics to simulation behavior and publish simulated sensor data back to ROS topics.

content.html:
Definition
Gazebo plugins
Plugins run inside Gazebo to control joints, sensors, and communication with ROS.
The differential-drive plugin subscribes to /cmd_vel and publishes /odom, acting as a translator between ROS and physics.
Sensor plugins publish streams like /scan and /camera/image_raw so other ROS nodes can subscribe and process data.
Sample plugin fragment
<gazebo>
  <plugin name="differential_drive_controller" filename="libgazebo_ros_diff_drive.so">
    <leftJoint>left_wheel_joint</leftJoint>
    <rightJoint>right_wheel_joint</rightJoint>
    <wheelSeparation>0.3</wheelSeparation>
    <wheelDiameter>0.1</wheelDiameter>
    <commandTopic>cmd_vel</commandTopic>
    <odometryTopic>odom</odometryTopic>
  </plugin>
</gazebo>
Pro tip
Start with a low torque value and increase while testing to avoid sudden unstable motion.

screens.title: Loading URDF and launching Gazebo
screens.subtitle: A step-by-step launch file workflow that spawns your robot

narration.text: To bring a URDF into Gazebo you follow a small launch workflow that loads the robot description into the ROS parameter server, starts Gazebo, and calls a spawn_model node to place the robot in the simulated world. The launch file in the chapter demonstrates this pattern: set the robot_description parameter to the URDF file path, include the Gazebo empty_world. launch to start the simulator, and call the spawn_model node with arguments pointing to robot_description, the -urdf flag, and initial coordinates. You also typically run robot_state_publisher so joint states are converted into TF frames and other ROS nodes can consume transforms. A concrete example is setting robot_description using a textfile param and then launching spawn_model with args -param robot_description -urdf -model my_robot -x 0 -y 0 -z 0.1. Common mistakes include incorrect file paths and forgetting robot_state_publisher, which results in missing TF frames. When you run the launch file, verify the robot appears in Gazebo and that TF frames such as base_link are being broadcast. This flow is repeatable and the basis for more complex world setups. Loading URDF and launching Gazebo means load robot_description, start gazebo, spawn the model, and run robot_state_publisher so tf frames are available.. In practical terms, a step-by-step launch file workflow that spawns your robot. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Launch workflow
keyIdea.text: Load robot_description, start Gazebo, spawn the model, and run robot_state_publisher so TF frames are available.

content.html:
Process Flow
Launch file steps
  1. Set robot_description parameter to the URDF text file.
  2. Include Gazebo's empty_world.launch to start the simulator.
  3. Run spawn_model node with args referencing robot_description and initial pose.
  4. Start robot_state_publisher to broadcast TF frames from joint states.
Lab check
After launching, confirm model appears and /tf contains odom→base_link transforms.
Example launch fragment
<launch>
  <param name="robot_description" textfile="$(find my_first_robot)/urdf/my_robot.urdf" />
  <include file="$(find gazebo_ros)/launch/empty_world.launch" />
  <node pkg="gazebo_ros" type="spawn_model" name="spawn_robot" args="-param robot_description -urdf -model my_robot -x 0 -y 0 -z 0.1" />
  <node pkg="robot_state_publisher" type="robot_state_publisher" name="robot_state_publisher" />
</launch>
Run with: roslaunch my_first_robot robot_gazebo.launch and watch for spawn messages and model appearance.

screens.title: Controlling the simulated robot with /cmd_vel
screens.subtitle: Publish velocity commands and observe motion and odometry

narration.text: Once the robot is spawned and a differential-drive plugin is configured, you control the simulated robot by publishing Twist messages on the /cmd_vel topic. The chapter demonstrates using rostopic pub with a geometry_msgs/Twist message to command linear and angular velocity. For example, publishing a positive linear x value moves the robot forward; a non-zero angular z value makes it rotate. The plugin listens to /cmd_vel and applies torques to the wheel joints accordingly, and it also computes and publishes odometry on /odom. A concrete command from the chapter sets linear x to 0.5 and angular z to 0.2; you should see forward motion and a slight turn. To validate, echo /odom to inspect pose and velocity or view TF frames for odom→base_link. A common misconception is expecting instantaneous perfect motion: simulation uses physics so acceleration, traction, and torque limits affect actual movement. If the robot doesn’t move, check that joint names in the plugin match URDF names and that the plugin is enabled. For practice, start with short commands and low velocities to confirm behavior before increasing speed. Controlling the simulated robot with /cmd_vel means publish twist on /cmd_vel; plugin converts commands to joint torques and publishes /odom so your control code sees feedback.. In practical terms, publish velocity commands and observe motion and odometry. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Control loop
keyIdea.text: Publish Twist on /cmd_vel; plugin converts commands to joint torques and publishes /odom so your control code sees feedback.

content.html:
Hands-on
Publish /cmd_vel
rostopic pub /cmd_vel geometry_msgs/Twist "linear:
  x: 0.5
  y: 0.0
  z: 0.0
angular:
  x: 0.0
  y: 0.0
  z: 0.2"
This command tries to move forward while rotating. Watch Gazebo and echo /odom to verify motion.
Validation & troubleshooting
  • Echo /odom to see pose updates and velocities.
  • Check TF frames to ensure odom→base_link is published.
  • If no motion, confirm plugin joint names match URDF and plugin is loaded.
Pro tip
Use short bursts of commands and inspect odometry to tune acceleration and torque values safely.

screens.title: Adding sensors: LiDAR and camera plugins
screens.subtitle: How to expose simulated sensor data to ROS topics

narration.text: Simulated sensors allow your ROS nodes to read realistic data without a physical sensor. In Gazebo, LiDAR and camera plugins produce topics such as /scan and /camera/image_raw which other ROS nodes can subscribe to. The chapter suggests adding a LiDAR via a gazebo_ros_ray plugin and a camera via a gazebo_ros_camera plugin. Configure the sensor’s update rate and topic names in the URDF or in sensor SDF tags so the plugin publishes deterministic data. A hands-on activity is to add a LiDAR to the robot URDF, launch Gazebo, publish /cmd_vel to move the robot, and concurrently run rostopic echo /scan to observe ranges as the robot approaches obstacles. For the camera, echoing the image topic shows raw messages; viewing in RViz requires an Image display. A common misconception is that simulated sensors produce perfect, noise-free data. Gazebo sensors are idealized unless you add noise models; when transitioning to hardware, expect additional sensor noise, latency, and calibration needs. Start with simple sensor rates and verify topics before integrating perception nodes so you can debug step-by-step. Adding sensors: LiDAR and camera plugins means use gazebo sensor plugins to publish /scan and /camera/image_raw, and remember simulated data is often cleaner than real sensors.. In practical terms, how to expose simulated sensor data to ros topics. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Sensor simulation
keyIdea.text: Use gazebo sensor plugins to publish /scan and /camera/image_raw, and remember simulated data is often cleaner than real sensors.

content.html:
Process
Add LiDAR and Camera
Attach a gazebo_ros_ray plugin for LiDAR. Configure topic name as /scan and an appropriate update rate.
Attach a gazebo_ros_camera plugin for a forward-facing camera that publishes /camera/image_raw.
In the lab: publish commands, inspect /scan and /camera/image_raw, and view images in RViz if available.
Example check commands
Use rostopic echo /scan to observe range arrays. Use rostopic echo /camera/image_raw or RViz Image display to inspect camera output.
Common pitfall
Expecting perfect data. Simulated sensors lack real-world noise and may require noise models for realistic testing.

screens.title: Simulation to reality: limitations and safety notes
screens.subtitle: How simulation differs from hardware and how to reduce surprises

narration.text: Simulation is a powerful development tool, but it is not identical to a real world. Gazebo models idealized physics: friction, motor characteristics, sensor noise, and contact response are approximations. When you transition to a real robot, expect differences such as increased friction, different motor response under load, sensor noise, and environment variability. To reduce surprises, follow systematic practices: start with conservative velocities and torques in simulation, tune inertia and friction parameters so the simulated dynamics roughly match expected hardware, and add noise models to sensors if you need robust perception testing. A concrete lab path is to test the obstacle avoidance node in simulation, then reduce speeds and re-run the code on the physical robot in a controlled environment. Always include emergency stops and soft limits in your control code. A misconception is that more complex simulation detail always improves transfer. In many cases, overfitting to a highly tuned simulator can harm generalization. Instead, use simulation for iterative development and safety testing, but validate on real hardware under controlled conditions before autonomous deployment. Simulation to reality: limitations and safety notes means use simulation for iteration and safety, but expect differences in friction, noise, and timing when moving to real robots.. In practical terms, how simulation differs from hardware and how to reduce surprises. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Simulation caveat
keyIdea.text: Use simulation for iteration and safety, but expect differences in friction, noise, and timing when moving to real robots.

content.html:
Process
From simulation to real robot
Simulated physics and sensors are approximations. Plan for friction, motor limits, and sensor noise when you move to hardware.
Start with low speeds and conservative torque limits both in sim and on hardware. Add safety checks and emergency stops.
Test incrementally: spawn, command, verify odometry, add sensors, then integrate autonomy layers gradually.
Why it matters
Prevents damage and builds confidence before field tests.
Practical step
Add sensor noise models or tune inertial values to better mirror hardware behavior.
Common pitfall
Overfitting to simulator detail makes real-world transfer harder; keep tests broad and incremental.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Three essential ideas to take forward

narration.text: Let’s summarize the core ideas you should remember. First, URDF is the robot’s blueprint: links and joints define structure, visual and collision geometry serve different purposes, and inertial values affect dynamics. Second, Gazebo is a physics simulator that uses URDF and supports plugins; plugins bridge Gazebo internals to ROS topics so controllers and sensors can be tested without hardware. Third, the gazebo_ros_diff_drive plugin subscribes to /cmd_vel and publishes /odom, letting you run the same control code in simulation and on a real robot. For each concept, practice by editing a URDF, launching Gazebo, spawning the robot, publishing a demo command to /cmd_vel, and observing /odom and sensor topics. Keep in mind the common contrast that simulation is a close but imperfect model of reality; always validate on hardware under controlled conditions before autonomous deployment.

keyIdea.title: Concise summary
keyIdea.text: URDF describes structure; Gazebo simulates physics; plugins connect simulation to ROS topics like /cmd_vel and /odom.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Key Concepts
URDF: links & joints
Describes kinematics, visuals, collisions, and inertia for simulation and TF.
Gazebo: physics sandbox
Simulates collisions, sensors, and dynamics so you can validate behavior safely.
Plugins: ROS bridge
Translate ROS topics to simulated forces and publish sensor outputs back into ROS.
Takeaway

Use URDF and Gazebo together to iterate quickly and safely, but validate with hardware before deploying autonomy.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 2
screens.subtitle: Three practical reminders for lab success

narration.text: A few practical reminders will help you avoid common pitfalls. First, always match joint names between the URDF and any gazebo plugin configuration. Mismatches are the most frequent cause of non-moving simulated robots. Second, simplify collision geometry to primitives wherever possible to keep the physics engine fast and stable. Third, use conservative torque and velocity limits early in testing and increase them only after validating behavior. As a short hands-on practice, spawn your differential-drive robot, publish a small /cmd_vel, echo /odom to confirm movement, then add a LiDAR plugin and verify /scan. Each quick check builds confidence and reveals naming or configuration mistakes early. Ask yourself after each run: did I see expected motion? If not, which piece of the pipeline — URDF, plugin, or launch file — likely needs inspection? These focused checks make debugging straightforward and keep your lab sessions productive.

keyIdea.title: Practical lab rules
keyIdea.text: Match names, simplify collision shapes, and test with conservative limits to iterate safely and quickly.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Key Concepts
Match URDF & plugins
Ensure joint and link names referenced by plugins match exactly those in the URDF.
Simplify collisions
Use simple boxes, cylinders, or spheres for collision geometry to keep simulation performant.
Start conservatively
Use low velocities and torques in early tests to avoid unstable simulation and hardware surprises.
Final takeaway

Simulation accelerates learning and reduces risk. Use URDF and Gazebo intentionally, validate frequently, and treat simulation as an approximation that helps you prepare for real hardware.
